claims.text: In equiatomic Nb-Ti-Zr-Hf-Mo, superconducting transition temperature is primarily governed by local lattice disorder through its effect on electron-phonon coupling.
Rapid quenching produces or retains a high degree of local lattice disorder in equiatomic Nb-Ti-Zr-Hf-Mo.
Annealing at approximately 1200°C followed by rapid quenching or slow cooling can provide a controlled comparison of cooling-rate effects.
Composition, annealing temperature, and ambient conditions are to remain constant while cooling rate is varied.
Changing the post-annealing cooling rate changes local lattice disorder and the associated strain distribution.
Rapid quenching preserves greater atomic disorder than slow cooling.
Greater atomic disorder alters local phonon modes.
The disorder-induced alteration of local phonon modes enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling increases the superconducting transition temperature.
Slow cooling permits partial atomic ordering.
Partial atomic ordering reduces electron-phonon coupling strength.
Slowly cooled, more ordered samples will have a lower Tc than rapidly quenched, more disordered samples.
The rapidly quenched sample is the baseline and is expected to retain greater local lattice disorder.
The proposed relationship is bounded to equiatomic Nb-Ti-Zr-Hf-Mo under the stated processing conditions.
Cooling-dependent grain-size variation could confound the inferred relationship between lattice disorder and Tc.
Thermal treatment may alter grain boundaries and microstrain, which may independently affect superconductivity.
XRD and TEM can be used to assess structural differences, while resistivity and magnetization can be used to determine and confirm Tc.
Failure of slowly cooled samples to show a statistically significant lower Tc is specified as a falsifying result.
A lack of meaningful cooling-dependent lattice-disorder difference is specified as a falsifying result.
